summary: A GitHub issue (ros2/ros2 #1514) opened by CraigBuilds on January 26, 2024, requesting a supported way to deploy ROS2 applications as standalone, self-contained packages on Windows, analogous to Snap on Linux. The author describes using pyinstaller and a virtual machine workaround, and rejects Docker due to cost and usability for non-developers. Maintainers and commenters discuss Robostack, colcon-bundle, msix_ros, and whether ROS2 is suitable for interoperating with closed vendor software given RMW and distro compatibility concerns.
one_line: GitHub issue requesting a Snap-like standalone deployment method for ROS2 applications on Windows, with discussion of pyinstaller, Robostack, and RMW interoperability.
key_facts: GitHub issue #1514 in the ros2/ros2 repository was opened by CraigBuilds on Jan 26, 2024 and had 13 comments.
CraigBuilds stated that deploying a ROS2 application as a standalone package on Windows is difficult and asked for a Snap equivalent for Windows.
The current workaround described by CraigBuilds was to send a whole virtual machine, or a physical computer, with the software installed to the user.
CraigBuilds reported that pyinstaller successfully ran rclpy.init() on the user's computer but failed during Node creation because it could not find the licence for RTI Connext.
CraigBuilds rejected Docker for Windows partly because Docker Desktop requires a paid subscription for companies with more than 250 employees.
CraigBuilds said the target users for deployment include robot operators such as a welding and cutting engineer or a crane operator, who should not need to know the software uses ROS2.
clalancette, a Contributor, said installing ROS 2 on Windows is very long, tedious, and error-prone, and suggested switching to Robostack as the most promising option.
clalancette noted that only about 30-50% of packages currently build on Robostack, and that Robostack supports only Humble at the moment.
mjcarroll suggested extending colcon-bundle, which he believed really only works on Linux, to other operating systems for runtime deployment.
CraigBuilds pointed to the msix_ros project (github.com/ms-iot/msix_ros) as another potential solution for deploying ROS2 on Windows.
traversaro argued that different ROS 2 versions or RMW implementations may not communicate appropriately, and that protocols like MQTT or OPC UA are typically used for integrating closed components.
gavanderhoorn wrote that it is too easy for ROS 2 nodes to embed implicit assumptions about a particular RMW, making a switch to another RMW non-trivial.
CraigBuilds stated that his team's standard is ROS2-Given-RTI-Given-Humble and that they plan to maintain a fork of Humble and the RTI RMW for long-term maintenance of about 50 years.
fujitatomoya questioned whether the Docker approach could start a ROS 2 application with a single command line, using the example docker run --rm ros:humble ros2 topic pub.
